# Dimension 6: Migration Patterns

Source details: [../citations.md](../citations.md)

---

## 1. The Modular Monolith Pattern

### Definition

A modular monolith structures an application as a single deployment unit while internally dividing it into distinct, loosely coupled modules. Each module encapsulates specific business functionality and interacts with others through well-defined interfaces [114].

"We rarely exchange the database access layer, logging library or GUI framework. For this reason, the module in the Modular Monolith is a business module" [114].

### Key Advocates

| Advocate | Contribution | Source |
|----------|-------------|--------|
| Kamil Grzybek | "Modular Monolith: A Primer" series + GitHub reference implementation | [114] [115] |
| Chris Richardson | Domain-driven modules based on DDD subdomains/bounded contexts | [116] |
| Spring Team | Spring Modulith canonizes the pattern in Java ecosystem | [117] |
| Google (HotOS'23) | Service Weaver: "write as monolith, deploy as microservices" | [23] |

### Shopify: The Canonical Example

Shopify Core is a modular monolith with 2.8M lines of code, 500K commits, and 1,000+ developers [13] [14]. Uses **Packwerk** to enforce module boundaries at build time [13]. On Black Friday: 284 million requests/minute, 45 million DB queries/second at peak [14].

Chose modular monolith over microservices: "their collective experience told them there is no one-size-fits-all solution" [13]. Certain components extracted only when "specific demands around scale, security, or isolation make it necessary" [13].

### Google HotOS'23 Paper

"Microservices conflate logical boundaries (how code is written) with physical boundaries (how code is deployed)" [23].

| Metric | Microservices (11 services) | Monolith (colocated) |
|--------|---------------------------|---------------------|
| CPU cores (10K qps) | 78 | 9 |
| Median latency | Higher | 0.38ms |
| Improvement factor | Baseline | 15x latency, 10x cost |

Led to open-source framework **Service Weaver** — write as monolith components, deploy as microservices [23].

### Academic Evidence

Systematic literature review (MDPI Future Internet, October 2025): From 369 retrieved records, only 15 primary studies were included, indicating academic research on modular monolith architecture "remains fragmented and lacks systematic synthesis" [16].

## 2. Fowler's MonolithFirst + Tilkov's Counterpoint

### MonolithFirst (Fowler, 2015)

Core arguments [1]:
1. **YAGNI**: "It may be hard to scale a poorly designed but successful software system, but that's still a better place to be than its inverse"
2. **Microservice Premium**: Only useful with more complex systems [2]
3. **Getting Boundaries Right**: "Any refactoring of functionality between services is much harder than it is in a monolith. But even experienced architects working in familiar domains have great difficulty getting boundaries right at the beginning"
4. **Execution Strategy**: "Design a monolith carefully, paying attention to modularity... it's a relatively simple matter to make the shift to microservices"

Fowler's own caveat: He'd "feel much more comfortable with this approach if he'd heard a decent number of stories where it worked out that way" [1].

### Tilkov's Counterpoint (2015)

Published on Fowler's own site as a direct rebuttal [119]:
- "If you are actually able to build a well-structured monolith, you probably don't need microservices in the first place" [119]
- "A monolith won't magically contain services waiting to be liberated" [119]
- Proposed **Self-Contained Systems** (SCS) as alternative — autonomous services larger than microservices [119]

### Current Resolution

The modular monolith movement has essentially become the practical implementation of MonolithFirst: start monolithic with strong internal boundaries, decompose later only if needed [1] [116].

## 3. Strangler Fig Pattern

### Origin

Coined by Martin Fowler in 2004 during a vacation in Queensland rain forests [120]. "Gradually create a new system around the edges of the old, letting it grow slowly over several years until the old system is strangled" [120].

### How It Works

A facade/proxy intercepts requests to the legacy system and routes them either to the legacy application or to new microservices. Over time, more functionality moves to new services until the monolith can be decommissioned [120] [121].

### Benefits

- Delivers value incrementally — "you benefit from microservices almost immediately" [121]
- Reduces migration risk — rollbacks are easier [121]
- "Gives you the flexibility to pause the modernization" for feature development [121]
- New features can be implemented directly as services [121]

### Risks

- **Proxy as SPOF**: "This proxy layer can become a single point of failure or a performance bottleneck" [121]
- **Data handling**: "One of the trickiest parts of the strangler pattern is handling data" [121]
- **Code base access required**: "You will need to make minor code changes and implement an anti-corruption layer" [121]

### Why Not Big Bang Rewrite?

"A big bang rewrite delivers no value until the very end when it's completed" and "is chasing a moving target" [122].

### Platform Adoption

Documented by AWS [123], Azure [124], microservices.io [121], and Confluent. Academic case study: IEEE Green Button System migration [138].

## 4. DDD and Bounded Contexts as Prerequisite

### Core Concept

"Bounded Context is a central pattern in Domain-Driven Design... DDD deals with large models by dividing them into different Bounded Contexts and being explicit about their interrelationships" [125].

### Bounded Contexts Are NOT Microservices

Vlad Khononov: "A Bounded Context is the exact opposite of a Microservice! A Bounded Context defines the boundaries of the biggest services possible" [126]. "If you follow the Bounded Context strictly, you will get monoliths. Those will be 'good' monoliths" [126].

### The Biggest Mistake

Microsoft Azure guidance: "The biggest mistake teams make when building microservices is splitting by technical layers — a service for the database, a service for the API, a service for notifications. This creates tight coupling and leads to distributed monoliths" [127].

Recommendation: "Split by business capability. Each microservice maps to a bounded context" [127].

### Implementation

Domain Events are local to a Bounded Context; Integration Events cross boundaries and should be "as small as possible" as they are "part of the contract made available by the given module" [137].

**Event Storming** is the recommended collaborative workshop technique to identify domain events, subdomains, bounded contexts, and aggregate boundaries before decomposition [137].

## 5. DHH's Majestic Monolith and Recovery Guide

### The Majestic Monolith

"An integrated system that collapses as many unnecessary conceptual models as possible, eliminating as much needless abstraction as you can swing a hammer at" [5].

"Run a small team, not a tech behemoth? Embrace the monolith and make it majestic" [5]. References GitHub and Shopify as monoliths with "millions of lines of code and thousands of programmers" [5].

### The Citadel Evolution

Keeps the Majestic Monolith at center, supported by **Outposts** — small extracted services for organizational, performance, or implementation reasons. Not full microservices; selective extraction only [129].

### Recovery Guide (5 Steps)

DHH's "How to Recover from Microservices" [128]:

1. **Stop digging** — no new microservices. Pick one existing service as epicenter to swallow others.
2. **Consolidate critical, dependent paths first** — signup, checkout, content viewing. "That's where microservices cause the most harm."
3. **Leave isolated performance hotspots for last** — narrow, isolated, performance-critical segments.
4. **Drop the most esoteric implementations** — consolidate to at most 2 backend languages.
5. **Partition with modules rather than networks**.

"The vast majority of systems should have no more than two backend languages: a general-purpose language tuned for programmer productivity for 99% of use, and a high-performance language for the last 1%" [128].

## 6. Successful Forward Migrations

| Company | Trigger | Result | Source |
|---------|---------|--------|--------|
| Netflix | 2008 multi-day outage | 700+ microservices, migrated to AWS (2009-2012) | [134] |
| Amazon | Marketplace scaling challenges | Two-pizza teams, "you build it, you run it" | [134] |
| Uber | Expansion beyond SF (2014) | 1,000+ services ("Death Star" architecture); built Uber Catalyst mesh | [134] |
| Agoda | GraphQL monolith complexity | Client-first approach: zero client-side code change during migration | [139] |

### Common Triggers

- Rapid growth outpacing monolithic architecture [134]
- Deployment bottlenecks — deploying everything at once [134]
- Scaling difficulties — inability to scale individual components [134]
- Need for independent team autonomy [134]
- Development velocity degradation as codebase grew [134]

## 7. Failed and Reversed Migrations

| Case | What Happened | Source |
|------|---------------|--------|
| HeartFlow | 9-month migration locked users out of healthcare portal on day one | [132] |
| Unnamed company | Migration "arguably was a key factor in killing the company involved" | [133] |
| Segment | 140+ services, 3-person team; "falling from the microservices tree, hitting every branch on the way down" | [12] |
| Amazon Prime Video | Step Functions hit scaling limit at 5% expected load; consolidated for 90% cost reduction | [9] [10] |
| Istio | Four microservices consolidated to single `istiod` binary | [130] |

### Common Failure Patterns

1. **Rushing without preparation**: Distributed architecture's complexity "not ideal for certain types of organizations" [135]
2. **Tight coupling preserved**: Teams maintain coupling from monolithic design across service boundaries [133]
3. **Wrong sizing**: Services too small = nanoservices; more services than can be managed [135]
4. **Data separation**: "Data separation is the hardest phase of any microservices migration" [28]
5. **Underestimating costs**: "Even if the microservices strategy turns out to be a success, it still means a heavy hit on the pocket" [19]
6. **Big bang approach**: "An incremental migration strategy prioritizing small, reversible changes is low-risk" [135]

Industry data: About **45% of companies** said they have had "some or no success" with microservices migration [135] (medium credibility — no primary survey source identified).

## 8. Reversibility: Microservices Back to Monolith

Peer-reviewed multivocal literature review (MDPI Electronics, 2024) documented four cases: Istio control plane, Amazon Prime Video, Segment, and InVision [15].

Five main reasons for switching back: **cost, complexity, scalability, performance, and organization** [15].

Six key aspects of the switching-back process [15]:
1. Stop developing more services
2. Consolidate and test paths
3. Unify data storage
4. Implement message bus principle
5. Give up diverse techniques
6. Learn modular design principles
